lines.text: Square windows made planes fall out of the sky.
lines.see: Tight on a passenger's face lit by a glowing square window, slow push onto the window's sharp corner

lines.text: This is the Comet. The world's first jet airliner. 1952.
lines.see: Camera slides out through the window: the whole silver Comet over a night sea, square windows glowing in a row

lines.text: Then, in 1954, two of them broke apart in mid-air.
lines.see: Headline 1954, the fuselage shudders and splits, debris drifts, the sea below

lines.text: Here's the weird part. Every flight, the cabin inflates like a balloon.
lines.see: Rewind to the intact plane, cutaway: the fuselage breathes outwards, amber pressure arrows push on the skin

lines.text: And that stress has to flow around every hole in the skin.
lines.see: Crane in on one window: amber stress lines stream along the skin and bend around the hole

lines.text: Round edges let it slide past. Sharp corners trap it.
lines.see: Split: on a round window the light glides past; on the square one it piles up white-hot in the corners

lines.text: So they sank a Comet in a water tank and pumped it, flight after flight.
lines.see: Pull out to a fuselage sunk in a tank of water, pulses of pressure, a flight counter climbs

lines.text: It tore open at the corner of a square window.
lines.see: Push into the corner: a crack races out from the sharp corner across the skin

lines.text: In testing, it lasted 16,000 cycles. The plane off Elba? 1,290.
lines.see: Headline 16,000 drops to 1,290, a counter bar collapses

lines.text: And that first crack started at a little square window in the roof.
lines.see: Crane up over the roof: two small square ADF windows glow, a crack runs from one corner

lines.text: Now windows are round. So, would you have boarded the Comet?
lines.see: Back on the passenger at a round window (loop to frame 0), stress glides around it, question headline

facts.claim: BOAC began the world's first scheduled jet airliner passenger service with the de Havilland Comet 1 G-ALYP, London to Johannesburg, on 2 May 1952
BOAC Flight 781, Comet G-ALYP (the same aircraft that flew the first jet service), broke up in flight and fell into the sea off Elba on 10 January 1954, killing all 35 on board

South African Airways Flight 201, Comet G-ALYY chartered from BOAC, broke up in flight near Naples on 8 April 1954, killing all 21 on board; the Comet's certificate of airworthiness was withdrawn and the fleet grounded

Investigators sank Comet G-ALYU in a water tank and pressurised it repeatedly; after 1,230 real pressurised flights and 1,830 tank 'flights' (about 3,060 in all) the fuselage failed at the corner of a squarish forward escape hatch window

De Havilland's prototype test fuselage survived 16,000 pressure cycles before cracking (it had been cold-worked by earlier 2P overpressure tests); production Comets formed fatigue cracks near window corners at about 1,000 flight cycles. The Elba aircraft had made 1,290 pressurised flights, the Naples aircraft 900

The Elba wreckage piece containing the two squarish ADF (Automatic Direction Finder) windows on top of the fuselage bore 'the unmistakable fingerprint of fatigue' and was the first fracture; the inquiry found the accident 'was caused by structural failure of the pressure cabin in the region of the A.D.F. window, brought about by fatigue'

Squarish windows created stress concentrations much higher than anticipated; on curved edges stress flows around with minimal build-up, at abrupt corners it cannot, and the window shape was later changed from squarish to the now-conventional oval
The Court of Inquiry report on G-ALYP and G-ALYY was published on 1 February 1955 and found failure of the pressure cabin due to metal fatigue from repeated pressurisation
